text: Every lesson in this chapter has assumed inference happens in a datacenter or cloud region. That's true for most large-model serving, but it isn't the only option. This lesson looks at the other end of the spectrum: running inference on or near the device itself, and when that trade-off actually makes sense.

Central serving means requests travel to a datacenter packed with GPUs, which is the default this whole course has assumed. It can batch requests from many users together, keep utilization high, and run as large a model as the budget allows. The cost is a network round trip on every request, data leaving the device to reach the model, and an outage affecting everyone at once.

Edge serving runs the model on or near the device — a phone's processor, a local gateway. It flips those trade-offs: lower latency since there's no network call, it can work offline, and data never has to leave the device. The catch is hardware: edge devices are far more memory and compute constrained, so edge models are almost always smaller and more heavily quantized, with a real quality ceiling.

Many real systems split the work instead of picking one side. The edge handles the common, latency-critical case locally; anything uncertain, or that needs a larger model's quality, escalates to the central service. Some organizations route by policy instead — certain data simply never leaves the device, regardless of difficulty.

Central serving wins on batching and raw capability; edge wins on latency, offline resilience, and privacy, at the cost of a much smaller model. Up next, lesson twenty-eight: what happens to all of this when traffic spikes far beyond what was planned for?
